title: Astronaut Moments: Chris Williams
description: Long before he became a NASA astronaut, Chris Williams learned through his time in Boy Scouts a very valuable lesson….“you can do a whole lot more than you think you can.”  The variety of accomplishments and skills acquired as a scout set a foundation of learning throughout Williams’ life, as he pursued a career in astrophysics, switched gears to become a medical physicist for cancer therapy, and now as an astronaut as he trained for his mission to the International Space Station.
keywords: Chris Williams, International Space Station, Expedition 74, Science, Radio Astronomy, Astronaut, Spacewalk
via: the NASA Image and Video Library

transcript.text: You know, I'm not entirely sure what
was the initial spark for wanting to join scouts, but,
my grandfather, had been involved in the Boy Scouts and when I was little,
I loved the idea of the outdoors and going
camping and kind of just this idea of, like, exploration.
As a kid, you got the opportunity to to be a leader.
So, you know, you as a middle schooler or high schooler were in charge of helping
to get another group of your peers, you know, successfully through a weekend
where you have to figure out what food you're going to bring.
Make sure that everybody has a place to sleep,
and make sure that you guys are all having fun.

to set these very clear goals, but also goals that are very achievable,
where you can learn
some really interesting things along the way, you know, merit badges.
And I remember, doing an astronomy and a space exploration
merit badge, but also in other areas, first aid...
That's a lot of just good life skills that, you know,
it kind of helps guide you towards which I thought was really fun.
And I really enjoyed doing ias a kid.
As a kid, I was always fascinated with space
exploration and understanding how the universe works.
I wanted to be a physicist,
so I wanted to study the stars, study astronomy and astrophysics.
So what is astrophysics?
To me, it really means using the laws and rules of physics
to try to understand and explain how the universe works around you.
So what I was working on for my PhD thesis was trying to build a new radio
telescope that could help shed some light on the first few hundred million years

so we could understand how that process happened.
So this is kind of, they call it the dark ages of the universe.
I jumped on with a group, at MIT that was working on this.
And, I loved working with radio telescopes and radio instrumentation,
and we were actually working on building a new radio
telescope out in the middle of the desert in Western Australia.
The idea to kind of go out into the field, work on building a new instrument,
to open up a new window on the universe just seemed really exciting to me,
even though a radio telescope that
may be a bunch of dishes or in the case of the experiment,
I worked on a bunch of just wire antennas laid out over the ground.
You can actually use math to turn those signals into an image
and a picture of the sky, which is absolutely fascinating.
After graduating from college,
I decided I wanted to do something to really give back
very directly to my community.
And there was a volunteer fire department down the street.
I worked as a volunteer firefighter and EMT for a little bit.
You know, I was finding a ton of satisfaction
in this volunteer work that I was doing where through medicine, I was being able
to really give back and help people on their worst day.
So I made a little bit of change in my career,
after graduate school and I, jumped into the medical physics career.
I said, maybe this is something where I can take my love and my passion
for physics and use it, to help people.
It was great because it had a ton of parallels to the work
I'd done in astronomy.
The math, for instance, that, you use to create an image from an MRI scanner

I had enough tools in my physics toolbox that even though I was using them
on the human body and radiation and the interaction of radiation
and cancer cells, like on the very small scale, my my education
and experience with the very large scale of the universe applied really directly.
One of the
things that I started learning at an early age through scouting,
but I think that also helped me in my career, was realizing
that you can do a whole lot more than maybe you think you can.
One of the things that I found the most interesting about the astronaut
training and training for a mission is how varied and different
the skills are that you need to learn to be successful on a mission
to the International Space Station.
You know, one day I'm flying in a trainer aircraft, learning how to work together
as a team with the other pilot and, and the air traffic control.
The next day, I'm underwater in a spacesuit,
turning bolts on a mockup of the International Space Station.
So every day is different.
I think that, you know, having something where you are exposed
to a lot of different things in a lot of different disciplines,
and you kind of prove to yourself that you can do it.
I think that helps a lot in approaching a job like this,
where you really have to execute at a high level
in a whole bunch of different areas, gives you the confidence

I think the thing I'm most looking forward to is to be able
to put all this training that I've done into practice
and to do the job that I've been training for and looking forward to,
you know, ever since I was a little kid.
I think the view people will not be so bad either.
I'm Chris Williams
and I'm a NASA astronaut.
